title: Therapeutic Communication: Listen Before You Fix
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: Therapeutic communication helps the patient describe experience, priorities, fears, and meaning without the nurse taking over the conversation. Use open questions, reflection, clarification, silence, validation of feelings, and concrete follow-up; avoid false reassurance, arguing, probing for curiosity, changing the subject, or giving personal advice.
recognize: Statements such as 'I'm scared this means I'm dying' usually need exploration and validation before education.
A patient who becomes quieter, more guarded, or repeatedly says 'never mind' may be responding to a blocking communication technique.
priorities: Create privacy and reduce distractions when possible.
Use open-ended prompts and reflect the patient's meaning before offering information.
Escalate immediately when communication reveals suicidal intent, abuse, acute confusion, inability to maintain safety, or other urgent risk.
assessMonitor: Assess understanding, emotional response, nonverbal cues, health literacy, language/communication needs, and whether the patient can teach back the plan.
interventions: Use qualified interpreters when needed rather than relying on children or untrained family members for sensitive clinical communication.
Use silence intentionally instead of filling every pause.
redFlags: Disclosure of abuse or immediate danger
Inability to understand essential safety instructions
teaching: Use teach-back to verify understanding without framing it as a test of the patient.
delegationScope: Supportive conversation is everyone's responsibility, but assessment of risk, capacity, acute mental-status change, and care-plan implications requires licensed clinical judgment.
examTrap: Responding to 'I'm terrified about surgery' with 'Don't worry, everything will be fine.'
oneLinePearl: Reflect the feeling, clarify the concern, then teach or act.

title: Documentation: Objective, Timely, Never Rewritten
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: The clinical record should show what was assessed, what happened, what was done, who was notified, and how the patient responded. Document objective facts and relevant patient statements promptly; never falsify, backdate, erase, hide an error, chart care before it occurs, or document another person's assessment as your own.
recognize: Words such as 'difficult,' 'noncompliant,' or 'seems drunk' are labels unless supported by specific observable behavior.
Late entries and corrections must follow the EHR/facility process so the original record remains traceable.
priorities: Chart patient care and response as close to the event as feasible.
Use objective observations, measurements, and exact patient statements when clinically important.
Correct mistakes transparently using the approved amendment process and escalate suspected record falsification.
assessMonitor: Confirm that high-risk events include required reassessment, notifications, interventions, and response rather than only the initial finding.
interventions: Use approved abbreviations and structured fields without allowing templates to insert findings that were not actually assessed.
Protect access credentials and never chart under another user's login.
medicationSafety: After a medication error, document the patient's clinical facts, assessment, interventions, notifications, and response in the health record; keep the safety/incident report separate according to policy.
redFlags: Record altered to conceal an error
Missing documentation of a major clinical change or required escalation
teaching: When documenting patient education, record what was taught, the learner's response/teach-back, and barriers or follow-up needs rather than writing only 'education given.'
delegationScope: Each person documents the care and observations they are authorized and responsible for; a nurse must not delegate professional accountability for nursing documentation.
examTrap: Deleting an incorrect entry so no one can see that it was changed.
oneLinePearl: Chart facts, actions, notifications, and response—and preserve the audit trail.
sourceBasis: The Joint Commission documentation and patient-safety principles

title: Intake, Output, and Fluid Restriction
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Intake/output is useful only when it is measured consistently and interpreted with weight, vital signs, edema, lungs, urine concentration, labs, and the patient's clinical condition. A fluid restriction includes all sources that count under the plan—not only drinking water—and should be divided across the day in a way the patient can realistically follow.
recognize: Unexpected positive balance with edema, crackles, rising weight, or dyspnea suggests fluid retention; low output with hypotension, tachycardia, dry mucosa, or rising creatinine may suggest poor perfusion or dehydration.
Ice, gelatin, soup, popsicles, liquid supplements, and fluids used with medications may count toward restriction depending on the care plan.
priorities: Measure intake and output using consistent units and time windows.
Obtain daily weights under comparable conditions when ordered because weight trend is often a stronger volume signal than one shift's I/O.
Escalate oliguria/anuria, acute dyspnea, rapid weight change with symptoms, severe sodium change, or hemodynamic deterioration.
assessMonitor: Trend weight, I/O, urine output, edema, lung sounds, BP, orthostasis, sodium/renal function when ordered, and adherence barriers.
interventions: Distribute the fluid allowance across meals, medications, and comfort needs.
Offer oral care, ice chips when allowed, small cups, and tracking tools to help manage thirst without covertly exceeding the restriction.
medicationSafety: Diuretics can change both output and electrolytes; interpret increased urine in the context of BP, weight, renal function, potassium, and symptoms.
Do not independently impose a fluid restriction on a thirsty patient without an order/clinical rationale.
redFlags: No or markedly reduced urine output
Severe confusion or seizure with sodium disturbance
teaching: Teach exactly what counts as fluid, how much is allowed, how to track it, and which symptoms mean the plan needs urgent reassessment.
delegationScope: Measurement may be delegated with clear definitions and reporting thresholds; interpretation of abnormal balance and clinical deterioration requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Recording only cups of water as intake while ignoring soup, ice, gelatin, and medication fluids counted by the restriction plan.
oneLinePearl: I/O is data; weight and the patient tell you what the data means.

title: Inhaler and Spacer Technique
bottomLine: Correct inhaler technique determines whether medication reaches the lungs. For a pressurized metered-dose inhaler, coordinate actuation with a slow deep inhalation or use a spacer/valved holding chamber when appropriate; dry-powder inhalers require a different, faster/deeper inspiratory technique and should not be treated like MDIs.
recognize: Common MDI errors include failing to exhale first, firing into the mouth without inhaling, inhaling too fast, taking repeated puffs with no interval, or not shaking/priming when the product requires it.
A patient may be labeled 'uncontrolled' when the actual problem is poor device technique or an empty/expired inhaler.
priorities: Identify the exact device before teaching because MDI, soft-mist, DPI, nebulizer, and breath-actuated devices differ.
Have the patient demonstrate technique rather than asking only whether they understand.
Clarify rescue versus controller medication and when worsening symptoms require urgent care.
assessMonitor: Assess inspiratory ability, hand-breath coordination, cognition/dexterity, spacer availability, dose counter, cleaning, adherence, symptom control, and rescue-use frequency.
interventions: For compatible MDIs, a spacer can reduce coordination demands and improve lower-airway delivery.
Rinse the mouth after inhaled corticosteroids to reduce local candidiasis/dysphonia risk.
medicationSafety: Do not use a long-acting controller as a substitute for the prescribed rescue strategy unless the patient's specific regimen intentionally uses an ICS-formoterol reliever approach.
Product-specific priming, shaking, breath-hold, cleaning, and storage instructions matter.
teaching: Use teach-back with the actual device at every opportunity; technique should be rechecked, not assumed permanent.
delegationScope: Routine reinforcement may be shared with trained staff, but assessment of uncontrolled symptoms, device mismatch, and medication response requires licensed clinical judgment.
examTrap: Teaching a dry-powder inhaler with the same slow inhalation technique used for a metered-dose inhaler.
oneLinePearl: Teach the device in the patient's hand, not an imaginary inhaler.
